sources.entry: Using load shedding to survive a success disaster - CRE life lessons

summary.name: Google SRE load shedding guide
summary.one_liner: A Google Cloud Blog article from the CRE life lessons series explaining how to use load shedding, dropping less valuable requests under overload, to keep a service available during traffic surges.
keywords: keep service available under heavy traffic
use_cases: Designing a service to stay available during unexpected traffic spikes
Deciding which requests to drop first when a system is overloaded
Setting per-client quotas that allow unused capacity to be used
Classifying background versus user-facing requests for throttling
Evaluating whether throttling signals a need for more capacity
summary.what_it_does: The article describes load shedding as serving nominal capacity regardless of incoming traffic by rejecting some requests and having clients retry. It covers a simple threshold-based approach that drops a fraction of traffic when CPU, memory or queue length exceed a load-tested safe level, and explains why ranking requests by criticality is better. It discusses measuring direct and opportunity costs, bucketing requests by criticality (via fields, hostname, URL path or user group), and dropping requests that exceed their deadlines. It also compares soft and hard quotas, optimistic versus pessimistic throttling, and includes a case study of a mobile upload service that survived a client bug.
notable: Case study of a Google mobile upload service that shed nearly half of background requests during a client bug
Explains soft versus hard quotas and work conservation
Compares optimistic and pessimistic throttling trade-offs
caveats: Describes general techniques and Google's internal practices; it is not a tool or product with an install or API
The Python example and simulation are described in the article but the code itself is not reproduced in the page text
Advice is presented as experience-based and may not fit every system
